lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Imagine a trading rule that returned nearly two hundred percent on one coin, while simply holding it lost about eighty. Is that a great rule?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It sounds amazing. But I'm guessing it's not that simple.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. Antoine's post scales up his BatchBacktesting engine to many tickers at once, stocks and crypto, with two strategies, and then reads the leaderboards honestly.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Because a single-ticker backtest flatters you. A big grid tells you whether a rule only works on one heroic symbol, whether disasters cluster in a sector or era, and whether crypto dominates just because volatility is unbounded in the simulation.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: An E M A crossover, buying when the twenty-period average crosses above the eighty-period one, with a ten percent stop loss and a twenty-five percent take profit. And a MACD crossover with no stop or take profit. Both use backtesting dot py.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The top EMA result was BTCBUSD at about two hundred ninety-four percent. The worst was BTTBUSD at minus ninety-nine point nine percent. Airlines and cruise lines showed up among the losers.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And that coin that beat buy-and-hold?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: OMGUSD. About two hundred percent with the rule, while buy-and-hold lost around eighty. The rule won by being short through a collapse. Meanwhile BTCBUSD went up under both, which says more about the period than the rule.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So high returns can just be luck or a long bull run.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. And before saying MACD beats EMA, he says compare the median return across all tickers, not only the top five.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Smoke tests. Find where a rule breaks, not where to put your money. It's not financial advice, and fees, halts and data quality all matter.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The full write-up has the charts and the code.
